The U.S. Department of Justice's Bureau of Justice Statistics (BJS), part of the Office of Justice Programs, has issued a notice proposing a new system of records titled "Bureau of Justice Statistics (BJS) Statistical Data, JUSTICE/OJP-017" pursuant to the Privacy Act of 1974. The system will maintain statistical data that BJS collects through questionnaires, surveys, interviews, focus groups, and administrative records in order to support its mission of collecting, analyzing, and publishing information on crime, criminal offenders, victims of crime, and the operation of justice systems at all levels of government. The records cover a wide range of individuals—including survey respondents, inmates, probationers and parolees, arrestees, and decedents who died in custody—and may contain sensitive information such as names, social security numbers, criminal history, medical information, and victimization details. BJS is legally prohibited from using this data for law enforcement, regulatory, or enforcement purposes, and must instead use it solely for statistical and research purposes under strict confidentiality protections found in 34 U.S.C. 10231(a), 34 U.S.C. 10134, and 28 CFR 22. The notice is effective upon publication, with public comments on the routine uses due by November 16, 2026.

summary_responses.response: This paper introduces DiffTry (Differential Retries), a mechanism that transforms standard retry operations into a prioritization system that protects high-value transactions from rejection during microservice overload periods. The core idea is simple: different priority classes of requests are assigned different retry-attempt limits—for example, premium users might get three attempts while low-priority users get only one—implemented in a lightweight, stateless, distributed design that requires no overload sensing or coordination between services. The authors develop analytical models that capture DiffTry's effectiveness, first for two services in tandem and then generalized to networks of services, proving convergence of their iterative solution approach and establishing monotonicity guarantees that success rates increase with retry limits. In their evaluation, high-priority transactions saw rejection rates drop to around 15% and accounted for about 85% of successful completions even when contributing only 50% of the input load, corresponding to a roughly 70% throughput improvement. The mechanism was validated through both simulations and a live Kubernetes deployment, where DiffTry functioned as a simple drop-in service-mesh plugin requiring no application changes, with measured rejection rates closely matching the theoretical analysis.

The statutory changes make virtually all Federal civilian service and certain honorable active military service qualify for determining FMLA eligibility.
The rule excludes certain Veterans Health Administration (VHA) employees covered by a leave system under 38 U.S.C. 7421 from title 5 FMLA coverage.

The December 2023 amendment allows honorable active service in the Army, Navy, Air Force, Space Force, or Marine Corps to count toward the 12-month service requirement for FMLA eligibility, but does not include service in the Coast Guard or commissioned corps of the Public Health Service.
The minimum qualifying service for FMLA eligibility under title 5 is 12 months.
